analogy.p: Imagine a bath being filled while the tap flow changes during the minutes. Plot the flow rate in litres per minute against time in minutes: the water in the bath at the end is the area under that graph, because each thin slice of time contributes flow × time. A steady flow gives a rectangle, a tap that opens steadily from zero gives a triangle, and a flow that changes irregularly is approximated by trapezia, one for each short interval. The analogy breaks down because a real bath has a plug and may leak, whereas the area method assumes every unit of rate is added to a total with nothing lost.
analogy.t: Filling a bath: the water collected is the area

bullets: **Calculate** the area under a graph made of straight lines: split into rectangles, triangles, trapezia.
**Estimate** the area under a curve: strips and trapezia (or rectangles).
**Interpret**: area under a velocity-time graph is distance; units come from multiplying the axes' units.
State whether an estimate is an **overestimate** or **underestimate**, with a reason.
Questions often give a table of values rather than a drawn graph, so be ready to use it.
Typical marks: 3 to 5, on both calculator and non-calculator papers.
The word 'estimate' tells you an approximate answer is expected and a range is accepted.
Link to other topics: area of triangle, rectangle and trapezium, speed-distance-time, units, rates of change.
core.h: What the specification asks you to do
core.p: Edexcel Higher asks you to **calculate or estimate areas under graphs**, including quadratic and other non-linear graphs, and to **interpret the results** in contexts such as velocity-time graphs and graphs in financial or other real-life contexts (this does not include calculus). For a straight-line graph you split the area into rectangles, triangles and trapezia and find it exactly. For a curve you **estimate** the area by splitting it into strips and treating each strip as a **trapezium**, then decide whether your answer is an **overestimate or an underestimate**. Crucially you must also say what the area means, with units, such as 'the distance travelled in metres'.

bullets: Area under graph units = (y-axis units) × (x-axis units).
Speed (m/s) against time (s): area = **distance in metres**.
Flow rate (litres/min) against time (min): area = **volume in litres**.
Acceleration (m/s²) against time (s): area = **change in velocity** in m/s.
Price per unit (£/kWh) against kWh: area = total cost in £.
A rectangle from a constant rate is the simplest case: area = rate × time.
The graph must start at the axis (the 'area under' is between the graph and the x-axis).
If part of the graph goes below the x-axis, that area counts as negative (for example moving backwards) at Higher level only when specified.
core.h: Why the area under a graph means something
core.p: The area under a graph is found by multiplying the values on the two axes, so it combines the two quantities. The **units of the area** are the **y-axis units multiplied by the x-axis units**. On a velocity-time graph with m/s on the y-axis and seconds on the x-axis, the area has units (m/s) × s = m, which is **distance**. This works because distance = speed × time: for a constant speed the graph is a rectangle whose area is exactly speed × time. For changing speed you add up many thin strips, each of which is approximately a rectangle or trapezium.

bullets: Rectangle: area = base × height (constant speed section).
Triangle: area = ½ × base × height (accelerating from 0 or decelerating to 0).
Trapezium: area = ½ (a + b) h (accelerating from a non-zero speed).
Example: speed rises from 0 to 12 m/s in 6 s: triangle area = ½ × 6 × 12 = 36 m.
Example: constant 12 m/s for 10 s: rectangle area = 12 × 10 = 120 m.
Example: speed falls from 12 to 0 in 4 s: triangle area = ½ × 4 × 12 = 24 m.
Total distance = 36 + 120 + 24 = 180 m; the figure shows this.
The base of a triangle or trapezium is **horizontal** time, not the slanted side, so do not use the sloping length.
core.h: Areas from straight-line graphs: shapes to know
core.p: When the graph is made up of straight lines, you split the area under it into familiar shapes and add the results. A **rectangle** has area base × height, a **triangle** has area ½ × base × perpendicular height, and a **trapezium** has area ½ × (sum of the parallel sides) × the distance between them. On a velocity-time graph with sloping and flat sections, the shapes are usually triangles (speeding up or slowing down from or to zero) and rectangles (constant speed). Always write each shape's area separately, then add, so that method marks are secured even if one number is wrong.

bullets: Area of trapezium = ½ (a + b) h, where a and b are the two parallel sides and h is the distance between them.
On a graph, a and b are the **heights (y-values) at the start and end of the strip**; h is the **width of the strip** (change in x).
Equivalent: area = width × average of the two heights.
Rectangle plus triangle proof: a h + ½ (b − a) h = ½ (a + b) h.
Each strip's area is calculated and then **added** to get the total.
For equal strips of width h: total = ½ h [y₀ + yₙ + 2(y₁ + y₂ + ... + yₙ₋₁)] (the 'trapezium rule').
The trapezium rule form is optional at GCSE; you can do each strip separately and add.
Do not use the sloping side as h; h is always perpendicular to the parallel sides (here, horizontal).
core.h: The trapezium formula on a graph
core.p: A strip under a graph with a sloping top is a **trapezium** whose parallel sides are the two vertical edges (the heights at each end of the strip) and whose 'height' h is the width of the strip along the x-axis. This can seem backwards, because on the graph the trapezium looks like it is lying on its side, but the formula is the same: **area = ½ (a + b) × h**. A good check is that it equals the rectangle of height a plus the triangle of height (b − a): a × h + ½(b − a)h = ½(a + b)h. Think of it as strip width multiplied by the **average height** of the two sides, which is why it is accurate when the top is close to a straight line.

bullets: Step 1: draw **vertical lines** to split the area into strips of equal width (unless the question tells you the strips).
Step 2: read the **y-value at each edge** of a strip.
Step 3: area of each strip = ½ × (sum of the two heights) × strip width.
Step 4: add all the strip areas.
Step 5: state units and whether it is an overestimate or underestimate.
With 4 strips under y = x² the estimate is 22; the exact area is 64 ÷ 3 = 21.3 (to 1 d.p.).
More strips give a better estimate; the exact area is the limit as strip width gets very small.
Show all heights and each strip's area in your working so method marks can be given.
core.h: Estimating the area under a curve with trapezia
core.p: A curve cannot be split into exact shapes, so you **estimate** the area by dividing it into vertical strips and replacing the curved top of each strip with a straight chord, which turns each strip into a trapezium. You then calculate the area of each trapezium and add them. **More strips** give a closer estimate because each chord stays closer to the curve. You read the heights at the edges of the strips from the graph or from a table of values, being careful with the scales. For y = x² from 0 to 4 with 4 strips of width 1 the heights are 0, 1, 4, 9 and 16, so the area is ½(0 + 1) + ½(1 + 4) + ½(4 + 9) + ½(9 + 16) = 0.5 + 2.5 + 6.5 + 12.5 = 22.

bullets: Curve **bends up** (convex): chords above the curve: trapezia **overestimate**.
Curve **bends down** (concave): chords below the curve: trapezia **underestimate**.
Reason must mention the straight line / chord lying above or below the curve.
Rectangles: using the **left** heights on a rising graph gives an underestimate, the **right** heights an overestimate (the reverse if falling).
Example: y = x² estimate 22 is more than the true 21.3: overestimate.
Example: a speed curve that levels off gives an underestimate with trapezia.
If the question says 'is your answer an overestimate or an underestimate?', you must give a reason to earn the mark.
A better estimate would come from using more (narrower) strips.
core.p: Whether a trapezium estimate is too big or too small depends on how the curve **bends**. If the curve bends **upwards** (convex, getting steeper, like y = x²) the chord between two points lies **above** the curve, so the trapezium contains a little extra area and you get an **overestimate**. If the curve bends **downwards** (concave, flattening, like a speed that levels off), the chord lies **below** the curve, so the trapezium misses a little area and you get an **underestimate**. A good exam answer says 'overestimate because the tops of the trapezia are above the curve' or the reverse.

bullets: Distance travelled = area under the velocity-time graph.
Average speed = total distance ÷ total time (here 180 m ÷ 20 s = 9 m/s in the figure example).
Constant speed: rectangle. Constant acceleration from rest: triangle. From a speed to another speed: trapezium.
If speed is in km/h and time in minutes, convert units before multiplying.
The area under an **acceleration-time** graph gives **change in velocity**.
For a table of values: treat each pair of consecutive readings as the sides of a trapezium.
If the car slows down to a stop, the final triangle has its height at the speed before braking.
The question may ask for 'how far' the vehicle travelled in a certain time: only use the part of the graph in that time.
core.h: Areas under velocity-time graphs: distance travelled
core.p: A velocity-time graph gives distance travelled directly from its area, and this is the single most common context in this topic. With straight lines you add triangles, rectangles and trapezia; with a curve you use strips. Once you have the total distance, you can also find the **average speed** as total distance ÷ total time. The units must be written: metres if speed is in m/s and time in s, or kilometres if speed is in km/h and time in hours. If the question gives a table of speeds at times, you can use equal strips directly between the table values.

bullets: Rate × time = total: area under a rate-time graph is the total.
Flow rate (L/min) × time (min) = volume (L).
Power (kW) × time (h) = energy (kWh).
Pay rate (£/h) × time (h) = pay (£).
Always use the **units on the axes** to decide what the area means.
If the time axis is in minutes and the rate is per hour, convert so that units match before multiplying.
The same trapezium technique is used whatever the context, so only the interpretation changes.
Link to other topics: compound units, unit conversion and rates.
core.p: Areas under graphs can represent amounts in financial and rate contexts. If the y-axis is a **rate** (for example pounds per hour, litres per minute or kilowatts) and the x-axis is **time**, then the area is the **total amount** accumulated, such as the total pay earned, the volume of water used or the energy used. As always the units are y-unit × x-unit, which gives the meaning: litres per minute × minutes = litres, kW × hours = kWh. You then use trapezia for a curved graph. Questions might give a graph of electricity use in kW against the hour of the day and ask for the total energy in kWh.

bullets: Strips can have **different widths** if the table has unequal time gaps; use each gap as its own h.
Area of each strip = ½ × (speed at start + speed at end) × time gap.
Check the table is in the same units as the answer needs.
Total = sum of all strip areas.
Describe how the values change to decide over or under (differences getting smaller means concave).
Example: differences in speed 8, 4, 2, 1 are getting smaller, so the graph flattens: underestimate.
If you only have 2 readings, one trapezium is still a valid estimate.
Use a calculator for the arithmetic but write down each term first.
core.p: Many questions give a **table of values** instead of a drawn graph, such as the speed of a car every 5 seconds. You treat each pair of consecutive values as the parallel sides of a trapezium whose width is the time gap. For times 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 s and speeds 0, 8, 12, 14, 15 m/s, the areas are ½(0 + 8) × 5 = 20, ½(8 + 12) × 5 = 50, ½(12 + 14) × 5 = 65 and ½(14 + 15) × 5 = 72.5, a total of 207.5 m. Because the speeds rise more slowly each time, the graph bends downwards, so the estimate is an underestimate. Writing each trapezium in a clear line avoids arithmetic slips.

bullets: More strips = narrower strips = closer estimate.
Reading errors from the graph make the final answer slightly out, and mark schemes allow for this.
The estimate with 4 strips under y = x² is 22; with 8 strips it would be 21.5, closer to 21.3.
A single trapezium for 0 to 4 would give ½(0 + 16) × 4 = 32, a poor estimate.
'How could you improve the estimate?' Answer: use more strips of smaller width.
Show every trapezium separately to earn method marks.
Use a ruler to draw the vertical lines, and read the heights from the scale.
Give the answer to a suitable accuracy with units.
core.p: The trapezium method gives an **estimate** because the real curve differs from the chords. The error shrinks as the number of strips increases, because each chord is shorter and nearer to the curve. In an exam, an estimate close to the true value earns the accuracy mark, and the mark scheme usually gives a range or follows through from your readings. A reading of the graph that is slightly off still earns method marks if the method is correct, so always show the heights you used.

bullets: Rectangle area = strip width × height.
Left-edge rectangles on a **rising** curve: underestimate.
Right-edge rectangles on a **rising** curve: overestimate.
On a **falling** curve the result is reversed.
The mean of the left and right estimates is exactly the trapezium estimate.
Rectangles are simpler but less accurate than trapezia for the same strip width.
Always read the question to see which method is asked for.
Example: y = x², 4 strips, left heights: (0 + 1 + 4 + 9) × 1 = 14; right heights: (1 + 4 + 9 + 16) × 1 = 30; mean = 22.
core.p: Instead of trapezia you may be asked to use **rectangles**. Each strip is treated as a rectangle with the height taken from the left edge, the right edge or the middle. On a rising graph, using the **left** edge heights gives rectangles that sit **below** the curve and an **underestimate**; using the **right** edge heights gives an **overestimate**. On a falling graph it is the other way round. Edexcel questions often ask for trapezia, but rectangle estimates can appear when a graph is described with step data, such as rates that change at set times.

bullets: 'Work out the distance travelled in the first 10 seconds': area from t = 0 to 10 only.
'Estimate the area under the curve between x = 1 and x = 5 using 4 strips': width 1, five heights.
'Is your answer an overestimate or an underestimate? Give a reason.' (2 marks)
'What does the area represent?' (1 mark): 'the total distance travelled in metres'.
'Work out the average speed': total distance ÷ total time.
'Explain how to get a better estimate': use more strips.
Link to other topics: area of trapezium, compound measures, graphs of quadratics.
Check units and the sensible size of your answer: the distance should not be larger than top speed × total time.
core.h: Typical exam questions and command words
core.p: Questions use **'work out'**, **'calculate'**, **'estimate'**, **'interpret'** and **'explain'**. 'Work out the distance travelled' on a straight-line speed-time graph means find the area exactly. 'Estimate the area under the graph' on a curve means use trapezia. 'Give a reason' for an overestimate wants a statement about the curve and chords. 'Interpret' wants the meaning in context: 'the area is the total distance, in metres, travelled in 20 seconds'. Many questions have two or three linked parts: area, then average speed, then over or under.

bullets: Convert units before multiplying (minutes to hours, km/h to m/s).
Read heights and widths from the axis **values**, not square counts.
The sloping side of a trapezium on a graph is not used in the area formula.
Base of the triangle on a speed-time graph is **time** and the height is **speed**.
Check each shape's area separately and add them.
Check the total against a rough rectangle for a sense-check (max speed × time).
Write the final answer with units such as m, km, litres, kWh.
If the graph has a negative part (below the axis), the question will say how to treat it.
core.h: Common pitfalls with scales and units
core.p: Marks are lost through unit and scale errors more than through arithmetic. If the y-axis is in km/h and the x-axis is in minutes, the area is not in km until you convert minutes to hours (or divide by 60). If the axis scales are not 1 square = 1 unit, you must use the axis values for the base and height of each shape, not the counts of squares. Writing out '½ × base × height' with the real values from the axes keeps you safe. Finally, check that your answer is believable: the area under a speed-time graph cannot exceed the maximum speed multiplied by the total time.

exam: 'Work out the distance travelled' (3 to 4 marks): identify the area under the graph (M1), calculate each shape (M1), add (M1), give the answer with units (A1).
Split the area into rectangle, triangle and trapezium and write each calculation on its own line, then add.
'Estimate the area under the curve using 4 strips' (3 to 4 marks): read heights (M1), ½(a + b)h for strips (M1), add (M1), answer (A1).
'Is your estimate an overestimate or an underestimate? Give a reason' (2 marks): 'overestimate' (B1) and 'because the chords lie above the curve' (B1).
'What does the area represent?' (1 mark): state the quantity and units: 'distance travelled in metres'.
'Work out the average speed' (2 marks): total distance ÷ total time, using the area already found.
'Explain how you could get a better estimate' (1 mark): 'use more strips', or 'use strips of smaller width'.
Show heights read from the graph clearly; a wrong reading can still earn method marks if the method is right.
Check the units on the two axes and give the area in the combined unit, converting where needed.
Give a sensible final accuracy; do not round the working values too early.
Look for the number of strips or the strip width in the question; if not given, you choose, so choose strips that line up with grid lines.
Do a sense-check: the area should be less than max height × total width.

mistakes.r: The height h in ½(a + b)h is the horizontal strip width; the parallel sides a and b are the vertical edges.
mistakes.w: Using the sloping side of a trapezium as the height in the formula.

mistakes.r: Use the values on the axes: area = y-value × x-value, with correct units.
mistakes.w: Counting squares without checking the scale.

mistakes.r: Triangle = ½ × base × height; trapezium = ½ (a + b) h.
mistakes.w: Forgetting to halve when finding the area of a triangle or trapezium.

mistakes.r: Give a reason: the chords lie above the curve, so the trapezia include extra area.
mistakes.w: Saying a trapezium estimate is an overestimate with no reason.

mistakes.r: The area is distance, so the units are metres (m/s × s = m).
mistakes.w: Giving the area under a speed-time graph in m/s.

mistakes.r: Convert so the x and y units match before multiplying.
mistakes.w: Mixing units (minutes and hours) when finding the area.

mistakes.r: Each trapezium uses its own strip width; add all the strip areas to get the total.
mistakes.w: Using the total time instead of the strip width for h.

mistakes.r: More strips gives a better estimate that may be larger or smaller, depending on how the curve bends.
mistakes.w: Assuming more strips always means a bigger answer.

mistakes.r: Say what the area represents, for example 'the distance travelled is 180 m'.
mistakes.w: Leaving the answer without stating what the area means.

summary: The specification asks you to calculate or estimate the area under straight-line and curved graphs (using rectangles, triangles and trapezia on strips), to say whether an estimate is an overestimate or underestimate, and to interpret the area in context, such as distance from a velocity-time graph. It matters because these multi-step estimate and interpret questions are worth 3 to 5 marks on Higher papers and test unit and scale skills.

terms.d: The area between the graph line or curve and the x-axis, found by splitting it into shapes or strips.
A quadrilateral with one pair of parallel sides; area = ½ (a + b) h.
The two sides of a trapezium that run in the same direction; on a graph these are the vertical edges of a strip.
A thin vertical slice of the area under a graph.
A y-value read from a graph at a particular x-value.
An approximate answer, as the area under a curve found with straight-line shapes is not exact.
An estimate that is larger than the true value.
An estimate that is smaller than the true value.
A straight line joining two points on a curve, forming the top of a trapezium.
A curve that bends upwards, with chords lying above it.
A curve that bends downwards, with chords lying below it.
The area under a velocity-time graph (units such as m).
Total distance divided by total time.
Units made by combining others, such as m/s or litres per minute, which multiply to give area units.
How one quantity changes compared with another, for example litres per minute.

worked.q: The graph shows the speed of a train. It goes from 0 to 12 m/s in 6 seconds, travels at 12 m/s for 10 seconds, then slows to 0 m/s in the next 4 seconds. Work out (a) the total distance travelled, (b) the average speed for the whole 20 s. [4 marks]
steps: (a) Distance = area under the speed-time graph. (M1)
(b) Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 180 ÷ 20. (M1)

worked.ans: Estimate = 22. It is an overestimate because the chords (tops of the trapezia) are above the curve.
worked.q: Estimate the area under the graph of y = x² from x = 0 to x = 4 using 4 strips of equal width. Say whether it is an overestimate or an underestimate and give a reason. [4 marks]
steps: Strip width = 1. Heights: x = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 give y = 0, 1, 4, 9, 16. (M1)
Check using the trapezium rule: ½ × 1 × [0 + 16 + 2(1 + 4 + 9)] = ½ × 44 = 22.
The curve bends upwards, so each chord lies above the curve and the trapezia contain extra area. (B1)

worked.ans: (a) 207.5 m. (b) Underestimate: the curve bends downwards so the chords lie below it.
worked.q: A car's speed v m/s is recorded every 5 seconds: t = 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 s and v = 0, 8, 12, 14, 15 m/s. (a) Estimate the distance travelled in 20 s using trapezia. (b) Is your answer an underestimate or overestimate? Explain. [4 marks]
steps: (b) The speed increases more slowly each time (gains 8, 4, 2, 1), so the graph bends downwards and the chords lie below the curve, giving an underestimate. (B1)
